items.explanation: The resolves open with compact theory: the states 'constituted a general government for special purposes,' delegating 'certain definite powers' and reserving the rest. The Constitution, in this telling, is a bargain among sovereign states -- not a grant of unlimited federal power, a foreign treaty, or an abolition of the states.
options: A. A grant of unlimited power to the federal government
B. A compact among sovereign states delegating only certain definite powers
C. A treaty between the United States and foreign nations
D. A document that abolished the state governments
items.stem: According to the resolves, the Constitution is best described as
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"Resolved, That the several States composing the United States of America, are not united on the principle of unlimited submission to their general government... and that in cases of a deliberate, palpable, and dangerous exercise of powers not granted by the compact, the States... have the right, and are in duty bound, to interpose for arresting the progress of the evil."
—Kentucky Resolutions, 1798 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The Resolutions say the opposite: the states 'are not united on the principle of unlimited submission to their general government.' Unlimited federal power is exactly what the compact theory denies.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Resolutions open with compact theory: the states formed a general government 'for special purposes,' delegating only 'certain definite powers' and reserving the rest — a bargain among sovereign states, not a grant of unlimited power.
option_explanations.C: The Constitution is not a treaty with foreign nations. It is the framework of the American government itself — the Resolutions treat it as an agreement among the states.
option_explanations.D: The Resolutions did not abolish the state governments; they presuppose them. The whole point of the compact theory is that the states remain sovereign parties to the bargain.

items.explanation: South Carolina tried to act on the 1798 logic in 1832, but Jackson's proclamation against nullification -- 'disunion by armed force is treason' -- backed by the Force Bill, showed the compact theory could not prevail against a determined president. The compromise tariff defused the crisis, but the theory's practical limit had been demonstrated.
options: C. The building of the Erie Canal
D. Jackson's threat of military force against nullification
items.stem: Which later development most clearly showed the practical limits of the Kentucky Resolutions' compact theory?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"Resolved, That the several States composing the United States of America, are not united on the principle of unlimited submission to their general government... and that in cases of a deliberate, palpable, and dangerous exercise of powers not granted by the compact, the States... have the right, and are in duty bound, to interpose for arresting the progress of the evil."
—Kentucky Resolutions, 1798 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The Louisiana Purchase (1803) was a triumph of federal power, not a test of compact theory — no state tried to nullify it.
option_explanations.B: The War of 1812 tested American arms and unity, but it did not put the Kentucky Resolutions' compact theory into practice.
option_explanations.C: The Erie Canal (1825) was a state-built internal improvement. It raised questions about federal versus state projects, but no state invoked compact theory to defy federal law over it.
option_explanations.D: Correct. South Carolina tried to act on the 1798 logic in 1832, but Jackson's proclamation against nullification — backed by the Force Bill's threat of military action — showed that a state could not defy federal law in practice. The compromise tariff defused the crisis, but compact theory's practical limit had been demonstrated.
